In June of 2024, staff were asked to report back to Council on their status of rent eviction
bylaws that have been passed in other Ontario municipalities.
In researching this report, staff learned from municipalities and we learned from data
from the Landlord-Tenant Board.
And we also learned from community-based tenant support and advocacy organizations, including
the City's lived expertise working group, and through an online eviction survey.
We learned about how rental renovation bylaws work and what they can and cannot do.
We learned that the experience of being evicted, whether lawfully or unlawfully, can be emotionally
traumatizing and economically devastating for that person being displaced.
We acknowledge the lived experiences that have been shared with us over the past few
months.

magnitude of this challenge in our community. Unlawful evictions due to renovations or rent
evictions occur in Kitchener like they do across Ontario. Tenant advocates are calling for local
governments to take action and the pathway staff are presenting are options for action that build
on the significant work that Kitchener is already doing in the space of affordable housing.
A decade ago, Kitchener recognized the need to play an active role in affordable housing
and a few years later, Council directed the preparation of Kitchener's first housing strategy,
Housing for All.
Path 1 contemplates a purposeful and continued focus on allocating resources and initiatives
and advocacy work that's already in our work plans.
This work is supporting the creation of new affordable and supportive housing,
supporting tenants and enabling more housing of all types in Kitchener.
This graphic provides an overview of the tremendous number of housing-related initiatives that have been approved, are in progress and are planned to occur.
We have challenged ourselves to do more and go further, and with the support of federal and provincial funding, we have done just that.
The City of Kitchener has seen the creation of over 1,000 new affordable units, including hundreds of supportive housing units.
And these efforts have helped to bring the purpose-built vacancy rate to a healthy 3% to 4% range in 2024,
which is a marked improvement over the vacancy rate of just 1% in 2022.
We know there's more to do.
The housing crisis is complex, and we continue to be committed to making a meaningful difference.
There are ways that we can intensify our efforts.
Path 2 actions leverage the expertise of others who are already working in the space and include
new initiatives that seek to support some of the same goals as a licence by-law.
Path 2 commits to developing tools to help tenants in understanding their rights and
community supports, developing tools to help landlords understand and uphold their responsibilities,
and to collaborate with community partners, the region and other area municipalities on
the actions and directions of the plan to end chronic homelessness and building better
futures.
Staff recommend that these initiatives be incorporated into Housing for All 2.0 so they
can be prioritized within the overall work plan and don't delay delivery of other corporate
priority projects.
As has been seen in other Ontario municipalities, licensing bylaws have been adopted to require
landlords to obtain a licence to renovate rental units when a tenant is being evicted.
A bylaw provides the opportunity to confirm compliance with provincial regulations, provide
a financial disincentive to landlords through fines and additional rent compensation payments
to tenants, provide proactive information and supports to tenants as well.
If such a bylaw is directed by Council, we need a made in Kitchener solution that doesn't
simply adopt the approach of another municipality but rather one that can be incorporated into
the City's structure and application processes with careful consideration of the resources
and complementary programs.
The preparation, implementation and enforcement of this type of by-law would require reprioritization
of existing housing work and dedication of new and additional resources.
Any by-law must work alongside the regulations of the Residential Tendencies Act and only
applies where an N13 has been issued and cannot stop an eviction.
Staff caution that by-laws in other jurisdictions are still in their infancy and their efficacy
cannot be confirmed.
Bearing on additional steps also has the potential to add complexity for tenants navigating an

work is already underway.

well as applying for and supporting community partners to access new federal and provincial
